newsitem.title: USA: U.S. imposes trade sanction on Argentina.
newsitem.headline: U.S. imposes trade sanction on Argentina.

text.p: The United States announced Wednesday that it will withdraw half of Argentina's duty-free trade benefits because Argentine laws fail to protect the intellectual property rights of U.S. drug companies.
U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshevsky said in a statement that the sanction would affect about $260 million worth of Argentine exports to the United States.
"We have seen some encouraging efforts on the part of the (President Carlos) Menem administration to establish modern intellectual property protection in Argentina," Barshefsky said in the statement.
"However, Argentina's resulting patent law and the new legislation designed to protect test registration data fall short of this objective and fail to meet international standards", she added.
According to Barshefsky, the new Argentine patent laws passed in 1995 and 1996 still allow Argentina's pharmaceutical companies to freely copy drugs developed by U.S. firms.
The United States has been pressing Argentina for years to reform its laws on intellectual property rights, which until 1995 set no restrictions on copying foreign drug patents.

Menem, who has sought to strengthen Argentina's diplomatic ties with Washington, proposed legislation that would have pleased the United States, but his bills were either blocked or watered down by the Argentine Congress.

In her statement, Barshefsky noted that "Argentine pharmaceutical interests continue to work aggressively to frustrate our efforts to achieve improved intellectual property protection in other countries".
The statement added that the final list of Argentine products that will be excluded from the U.S. Generalized System of Preferences (GSP) will be published "on or about March 1".
A USTR spokesman said the sanctions would be imposed on manufactured goods, as the GSP excludes commodities.
President Clinton advised Menem of his decision in a letter made public Tuesday in Buenos Aires.
